issues.legal_issue: A representative suit seeking recovery of trust property is governed by the limitation rule for possession rather than the rule for a mere declaration.
material_facts: Creditors brought a representative suit seeking a declaration that transferred properties remained subject to a trust, appointment of an administrator, and recovery of the properties into the administrator’s possession.
The suit was valued as a claim for possession, and defendants in possession were joined on that basis.
issues.conclusion: Read as a whole, the suit sought possession as well as a declaration and was governed by Article 134, not Article 120, of the Limitation Act; it was therefore within time.
issues.legal_principle: The applicable limitation article depends on the plaint read as a whole and properly construed, including the substance of the relief sought rather than its form. A suit seeking possession of property for delivery to a newly appointed administrator is not a mere declaratory suit. The Court distinguished the rule in Rani Chhatra Kumari Devi v. Prince Mohan Bikram Shah, which concerned a beneficiary’s claim to possession as owner.

predicates.representative_trust_suit: Creditors brought the suit on behalf of a general body of creditors under a representative procedure.
predicates.seeks_recovery_of_trust_property: The plaintiffs sought recovery of trust property into the possession of an administrator.
predicates.suit_valued_as_possession_claim: The plaintiffs valued the suit on the basis that possession of the properties was sought.

issues.definition: When a representative trust suit seeks recovery of property and is valued as a possession claim, the claim is treated as timely under the limitation rule applicable to possession.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary of a private trust may seek recovery of improperly alienated property into the possession of a replacement trustee, and the statutory remedies for a declaration are not exhaustive.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought removal of the surviving trustee, appointment of an administrator, and recovery of properties allegedly alienated improperly by the trustees.
The plaintiffs sought delivery of the properties to the administrator rather than claiming possession as owners.
issues.conclusion: The claim for recovery of the properties into the administrator’s possession was competent; section 63 of the Indian Trusts Act did not exhaust the beneficiary’s remedies or prohibit a claim for constructive possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Trusts Act provides for requiring an alienee to admit that property is comprised in a trust or suing for a declaration to that effect, but is not exhaustive of a beneficiary’s remedies. Section 10 of the Limitation Act contemplates following trust property and seeking its delivery to a new trustee. The Court considered A. Subramania Iyer v. P. Nagarathna Naicker, Masjid Shahid Ganj v. Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, Subbaiya Pandaram v. Mahamad Mustapha Maracayar, and distinguished Rani Chhatra Kumari Devi v. Prince Mohan Bikram Shah.

predicates.private_trust_beneficiary_suit: Beneficiaries brought a suit concerning property held under a private trust.
predicates.seeks_recovery_to_replacement_trustee: The beneficiaries sought delivery of the property to a replacement trustee or administrator.
predicates.property_allegedly_improperly_alienated: The beneficiaries alleged that the existing trustee had improperly alienated trust property.

issues.definition: A beneficiary suing over allegedly misalienated private-trust property may seek its recovery to a replacement trustee when that is the relief sought.

issues.legal_issue: Withdrawal of a suit brought by debtors does not bar a later representative suit brought by creditors who are neither the same parties nor claiming through the earlier plaintiffs.
material_facts: The debtors had previously brought an administration suit and later withdrew it.
Creditors subsequently pursued the present suit in their representative capacity under Order I, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The creditors were not the same parties as the debtors in the earlier suit and did not claim through them.
issues.conclusion: The later representative suit was not barred by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs the plea of res judicata in a suit. Where the parties in the later suit are not the same parties as, or persons claiming through, the parties to the earlier suit, section 11 does not bar the later suit; a general doctrine of res judicata cannot be invoked in its place.

predicates.later_representative_suit: The later suit was brought by claimants in a representative capacity on behalf of a wider group.
predicates.earlier_suit_withdrawn: The plaintiffs in an earlier suit withdrew that suit.
predicates.later_claimants_not_same_or_claiming_thr: The claimants in the later suit were not the same parties as, and did not claim through, the plaintiffs in the earlier suit.

issues.definition: A withdrawn earlier suit does not bar a later representative suit when its claimants are not the same parties as, or claiming through, the earlier plaintiffs.

issues.legal_issue: A sale of trust property executed by only some of multiple trustees is invalid when the trust instrument requires all trustees to act, even though decisions may be made by majority.
material_facts: The trust deed appointed three trustees and provided that they were to act either unanimously or according to a majority decision.
Two of the trustees executed the challenged sale deeds, while the third did not join in executing them.
The trust deed did not provide that fewer than all trustees could execute the trust.
issues.conclusion: The deeds executed by only two of the three trustees were invalid and conveyed no title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Indian Trusts Act requires all trustees to join in executing the trust unless the trust instrument provides otherwise. A clause permitting decisions by majority does not, without more, permit a majority of trustees to carry out the resulting action without the others. The Court relied on Lala Man Mohan Das v. Janki Prasad.

predicates.multiple_trustees: The trust was administered by more than one trustee.
predicates.trust_instrument_requires_all_to_act: The trust instrument required all trustees to act in carrying out the trust, although decisions could be made by majority.
predicates.deed_executed_by_fewer_than_all_trustees: Fewer than all of the trustees executed the deed transferring trust property.

issues.definition: A transfer is ineffective when multiple trustees are required to act together but fewer than all execute it.

issues.legal_issue: A non-signing trustee’s approval does not validate a transfer unless the trustee’s consent or approval is established by evidence.
material_facts: Two trustees executed a sale deed without the third trustee’s signature.
The alienees argued that the third trustee had consented to the transaction.
The trial court and High Court found that the third trustee was not a consenting party, and the evidence did not establish his approval.
issues.conclusion: The asserted consent of the third trustee could not validate the deed because it was not proved.
issues.legal_principle: An act by some trustees may be treated as the act of all if the other trustee sanctioned or approved it, but that sanction or approval must be strictly proved. The Court accepted the concurrent factual finding that consent had not been established.

predicates.trust_deed_executed_by_some_trustees: Some, but not all, trustees executed a deed concerning trust property.
predicates.non_signing_trustee_approval_asserted: A party asserted that a trustee who did not sign the deed had approved the transaction.
predicates.approval_not_proved: The evidence did not establish that the non-signing trustee approved the transaction.

issues.definition: An asserted approval by a non-signing trustee cannot validate a deed when the approval is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A court may correct an obvious error in its formal decree under its inherent and correction powers even after an appeal from the decree has been admitted.
material_facts: The formal decree used the words “mesne profits,” although the judgment and the trial court’s decree referred to “net profits.”
The High Court corrected the wording under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure after appeals had been admitted by the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to correct the obvious error in the decree despite the admission of the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit correction of an obvious error in a formal decree so that it conforms to the judgment, including where an appeal has already been admitted. The change corrected an inadvertent discrepancy rather than altering the court’s decision.

predicates.formal_decree_contains_obvious_inadverte: The formal decree contains wording that is an obvious inadvertent error.
predicates.correction_makes_decree_conform_to_judgm: The proposed correction makes the decree reflect the decision actually expressed in the judgment.
predicates.appeal_already_admitted: An appeal from the decree had been admitted before the correction was made.

issues.definition: A court may correct an obvious, inadvertent mismatch between its decree and judgment even after an appeal has been admitted.

issues.legal_issue: Net profits may be ordered as part of an equitable adjustment between a trust and an alienee whose transfer is set aside, notwithstanding the ordinary limitation on a claim for profits.
material_facts: The transfers to the alienees were set aside, but the alienees were allowed recovery of amounts due to them from the trust with interest.
The decree also required the alienees to account for net profits from the properties during their possession.
The directions for payment and accounting were made together to adjust the equities between the trust and the alienees.
issues.conclusion: The direction to account for net profits was an equitable adjustment and was not defeated by the ordinary three-year limitation applicable to claims for profits under Article 109 of the Limitation Act.
issues.legal_principle: Article 109 of the Limitation Act ordinarily limits a claim for profits wrongfully received from immovable property. However, a court may make an equitable adjustment between parties by linking an alienee’s recovery of money and interest to the alienee’s accounting for net profits. The Court relied on Satgur Prasad v. Har Narain Das and Bhagwat Dayal Singh v. Debi Dayal Sahu.

predicates.trust_property_transfer_set_aside: A transfer of trust property was set aside.
predicates.alienee_awarded_reimbursement_with_inter: The alienee was allowed recovery from the trust of money due, together with interest.
predicates.profit_accounting_forms_part_of_equitabl: The accounting for profits was linked to the reimbursement and interest as part of an equitable adjustment between the parties.

issues.definition: When reimbursement and interest are allowed to an alienee whose transfer is set aside, net-profit accounting may be ordered as part of the same equitable adjustment.

issues.legal_issue: A court making an equitable adjustment may award simple interest rather than the contractual compound rate applicable to a mortgage.
material_facts: The alienee relied on a mortgage stipulating compound interest.
The decree allowing recovery of the mortgage debt was made in the trust suit to adjust equities after the transfer was set aside, not in an action brought by the alienee as mortgagee.
The High Court substituted simple interest for compound interest.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could award simple interest as part of the equitable adjustment, and its modification was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A mortgagee is ordinarily entitled to contractual interest in a mortgage action, as recognized in Jagannath Prasad Singh Chowdhury v. Surajmal Jalal. But when recovery is granted as equitable relief in an action setting aside an alienation, the court may determine the appropriate interest as part of its equitable adjustment rather than apply the contractual compound rate.

predicates.recovery_awarded_as_equitable_relief: The court allowed recovery of a debt as equitable relief in adjusting the parties’ rights.
predicates.claim_not_brought_as_mortgage_action: The proceeding was not an action brought by the claimant to enforce the mortgage as mortgagee.

issues.definition: When debt recovery is granted as equitable relief outside a mortgage action, the court may use simple interest in its adjustment.

issues.legal_issue: A person who intermeddles with trust property and takes an active role in administering the trust may become a trustee de son tort, making a transfer of trust property to that person invalid.
material_facts: The purchaser directed a clerk of the trust estate, corresponded with creditors and a bank about settlement of trust debts, entered into compromises concerning estate obligations, and dealt with estate receipts.
He continued these activities after ceasing to be a creditor of the estate.
He entered into possession of the property years before the sale deed in his favour was executed.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was a trustee de son tort, and the sale deed in his favour was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Even slight intermeddling with trust property may make a person a trustee de son tort; sustained and active involvement in administering the trust estate is sufficient. The Court referred to the principle stated in Williams on Executors and Administrators.

predicates.person_intermeddles_with_trust_estate: A person dealt with trust property or estate affairs without being authorized as a trustee.
predicates.person_takes_active_role_in_trust_admini: The person actively directed or handled matters involved in administering the trust estate.
predicates.transfer_made_to_that_person: Trust property was transferred to that person.

issues.definition: A transfer to a person who actively intermeddles in administering the trust estate is invalid when the person acquires the property.

issues.legal_issue: Trustees charged with selling trust property cannot use the sale to benefit themselves indirectly or delegate their sale duties to a purchaser when the trust instrument does not authorize delegation.
material_facts: The trustees were required to sell trust properties at the best obtainable price and distribute the proceeds among creditors.
Some properties were transferred to close relatives of one trustee.
A transaction involved a purchaser being left to sell properties to creditors and satisfy their claims, rather than the trustees themselves carrying out their duties.
The evidence concerning the grouped sale showed that the properties had not been individually valued and the purchaser had not inspected or assessed them.
issues.conclusion: The challenged transactions involving the trustee’s relatives were invalid, including the transaction that improperly delegated the trustees’ functions to a purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Indian Trusts Act prohibits a trustee whose duty is to sell trust property from buying it, directly or indirectly, for the trustee’s own account or as an agent for another. Section 47 prohibits delegation of a trustee’s office or duties except in the specified circumstances. The Court also relied on Lewin on Trusts concerning a trustee’s disability from purchasing trust property.

predicates.trustees_have_duty_to_sell_for_best_pric: The trustees were responsible for selling trust property for the best obtainable price and applying the proceeds to the trust’s purposes.
predicates.trustee_benefits_indirectly_through_rela: Property was transferred to a close relative of a trustee in circumstances in which the trustee benefited indirectly from the purchase.
predicates.sale_duties_delegated_to_purchaser: The trustees left the purchaser to perform duties involved in selling the trust property or satisfying the trust’s creditors.

issues.definition: A transaction is invalid when trustees charged with selling property for the trust use a related purchaser to benefit indirectly or delegate their sale duties without authority.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer granted as compensation for loss under an earlier invalid transaction is itself invalid when its foundation is an invalid transaction and the claimed loss was not established.
material_facts: A purchaser received a later deed for property as compensation for the loss of other property conveyed under an earlier grouped sale.
The earlier sale involved numerous properties sold together without serious individual valuation, and the purchaser had not inspected or assessed them.
The purchaser had not refunded the money to the creditor whose property was involved in the alleged loss.
issues.conclusion: The later deed was invalid because it depended on the earlier invalid transaction and the basis for the claimed compensation was not established.
issues.legal_principle: A transaction that rests on an earlier transaction may fail when the earlier transaction is invalid. The Court found that the earlier sale was invalid because of inadequate valuation and impermissible delegation, and also noted that the purchaser had not refunded the money said to support the later transfer.

predicates.later_transfer_given_as_compensation_for: A later transfer was made to compensate a purchaser for an alleged loss under an earlier transaction.
predicates.earlier_transaction_invalid: The earlier transaction on which the later transfer depended was invalid.
predicates.claimed_loss_not_established: The evidence did not establish the loss said to justify the later transfer.

issues.definition: A later transfer given as compensation is invalid when its underlying transaction is invalid and the asserted loss is unestablished.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that trust property was transferred for grossly inadequate consideration will be upheld when the supporting evidence remains unrebutted.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court found that properties transferred to a purchaser were sold for grossly inadequate consideration.
The purchaser did not testify to rebut the plaintiffs’ evidence.
The valuation findings were based on documentary and oral evidence, and the asserted error in the courts’ treatment of the land categories was not supported by the judgments.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings of inadequate consideration were upheld, and the challenge to the transfers failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the concurrent factual findings of the lower courts where the evidence supporting inadequate consideration remained unrebutted and the suggested error in the valuation analysis was not borne out by the record.

predicates.appeal_challenges_concurrent_valuation_f: An appeal challenged valuation findings reached by both the trial court and the appellate court.
predicates.evidence_of_inadequate_price_unrebutted: Evidence that the property was sold for an inadequate price remained unrebutted.
predicates.alleged_valuation_error_not_supported_by: The claimed error in the valuation analysis was not supported by the record.

issues.definition: Concurrent findings of inadequate consideration are upheld when their evidentiary basis remains unrebutted and the asserted valuation error is unsupported.
